summary:
LMBS – Lunar & Mars Base Survival is an educational 3D space-survival game for children aged 7–12. Players choose Captain Alex or Captain Luna and run a base on the Moon, Mars, and Europa, managing limited oxygen, energy, food, water, and shielding in real time. When a resource runs out, the crew’s hearts are lost, so every decision has a visible cost and consequence.

The game addresses the challenge of making space science engaging and understandable for young learners. It uses real NASA DONKI space-weather data, such as solar flares and CMEs, to trigger learning scenarios, and it clearly separates real data from labeled simulation. ROBO-X, an AI assistant built on retrieval from trusted sources, explains concepts in simple language and says “I’m not sure” rather than inventing answers.

It matters because future space exploration depends on people who understand resource limits, risk, and teamwork. LMBS turns that understanding into play and inspires the next generation of explorers. Its core lesson is that there is no free decision in space.

details:
How it works

LMBS is a web-based 3D survival game. After signing up (or playing as a guest), the player picks Captain Alex or Captain Luna, watches a mission briefing, and starts on the Moon. They run around the base in real time and use zones such as the oxygen generator, solar panels, water tank, and farm. The resources are Oxygen, Energy, Food, Water, and Shield, and each one is produced, consumed, and linked to the others. For example, the oxygen generator needs energy, and the farm needs energy and water. A seeded simulation engine on the server calculates every change and gives a reason for it. If a resource hits zero, the crew loses a heart, and with no hearts left the mission fails and can be retried. Players earn 1–3 stars based on decision quality, and they unlock Mars and then Europa. Each world has different conditions: dust storms and communication delay on Mars, extreme cold and radiation on Europa. Fictional alien thieves try to steal supplies, and the player can chase them or choose a defense. A results screen explains what the player learned from their own decisions.

Benefits and intended impact

Children learn that resources in space are limited and that every choice has a cost. They learn this by playing instead of reading. The game is meant to build interest in space science and systems thinking, and to encourage the next generation of explorers. ROBO-X, the AI assistant, helps players understand their mistakes in simple language.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite
  • 3D: three.js and React Three Fiber, with animated GLB character models
  • Backend: Node.js and Express, with a SQLite database
  • Security: bcrypt password hashing, cookie sessions, Zod input validation, and an admin dashboard with its own login
  • AI: Gemini API, used server-side only, with retrieval from a trusted knowledge base (RAG)
  • Data: NASA DONKI API for real solar events
  • Testing: Node’s built-in test runner and Playwright
  • Development: Google AI Studio

Creativity

The game turns real NASA space-weather events into playable scenarios. It also separates real data from simulation. Every value is labeled as either “NASA data” or “Clearly Labeled Simulation,” and the aliens are marked as fictional. ROBO-X says “I’m not sure” when it has no reliable source, instead of making up an answer. The difficulty comes from each world’s real environmental conditions, not from bigger numbers.

Factors we considered

  • Child safety: nicknames only on the leaderboard, minimal data collection, no IP or device tracking, and account deletion.
  • Honesty: cached or archived NASA data is never shown as live.
  • Fairness: the server controls stars, XP, and resources, so players can’t cheat from the browser.
  • Reliability: the game stays playable if NASA or the AI is unavailable.
  • Accessibility: status uses color plus icon plus text, with reduced-motion and low-graphics modes, and the layout works on mobile.
